Complexity Measures for Imbalanced Classification Data

complexity_measures.Rd

Measures of the class imbalance, of the class overlap and of the noise of a classification data set, taken from the literature. Higher values mean a more imbalanced or a more complex (harder) problem. Each measure is a function of its own; complexity calculates all of them or the selected ones.

Usage

complexity_IR(x = NULL, y)

complexity_C1(x = NULL, y)

complexity_C2(x = NULL, y)

complexity_ID(x = NULL, y)

complexity_F1(x, y)

complexity_F1v(x, y)

complexity_F2(x, y)

complexity_F3(x, y)

complexity_F4(x, y)

complexity_N1(x, y, scale = "minmax")

complexity_N2(x, y, scale = "minmax")

complexity_N3(x, y, scale = "minmax")

complexity_N3_bal(x, y, scale = "minmax")

complexity_N4(x, y, scale = "minmax", seed = NULL)

complexity_LSC(x, y, scale = "minmax")

complexity_R(x, y, k = 7, theta = 3, scale = "minmax")

complexity_R_aug(x, y, k = 7, theta = 3, scale = "minmax")

complexity_SAFE(x, y, k = 5, scale = "minmax")

complexity_BORDERLINE(x, y, k = 5, scale = "minmax")

complexity_RARE(x, y, k = 5, scale = "minmax")

complexity_OUTLIER(x, y, k = 5, scale = "minmax")

Arguments

x

feature matrix or data.frame (numeric).

y

a factor class variable. Can have more than two classes (see Details).

scale

scaling of the features before distances are calculated: "minmax" (default, to [0, 1]), "zscore" or "none". Feature based measures (F1, F1v, F2, F3, F4) use the original features.

seed

seed of the random interpolation of N4. Default is NULL (the random number stream is not touched).

k

number of nearest neighbors. Default is 7 for R and R_aug (Oh, 2011) and 5 for the types of minority examples (Napierala & Stefanowski, 2016).

theta

threshold of the R-value: a sample is in the overlapping region if more than theta of its k nearest neighbors are from other classes. Default is 3.

Value

a number.

Details

Class imbalance (they use y only; x may be NULL):

  • IR: imbalance ratio, size of the largest class divided by the size of the smallest class.

  • C1: \(1 + \sum_k p_k \log p_k / \log K\), one minus the normalized entropy of the class proportions \(p_k\) (Lorena et al., 2019). 0 means balanced, 1 means one class has all the samples.

  • C2: \(1 - 1 / IR_{K}\) with \(IR_{K} = \frac{K - 1}{K} \sum_k n_k / (n - n_k)\) (Lorena et al., 2019).

  • ID: imbalance degree (Ortigosa-Hernandez et al., 2017), with the Euclidean distance. 0 means balanced; the integer part is the number of minority classes minus one.

Overlap, feature based (Ho & Basu, 2002; Lorena et al., 2019). They are defined for two classes; with more classes the mean over all pairs of classes (one-versus-one) is returned. They are transformed so that higher means more overlap:

  • F1: \(1 / (1 + r)\), with \(r\) the maximum Fisher's discriminant ratio over the features. F1v: the same with the directional (vector) Fisher's ratio (Orriols-Puig et al., 2010).

  • F2: volume of the overlapping region (product over the features of the relative overlap).

  • F3: maximum individual feature efficiency, inverted: the smallest proportion of samples in the overlapping interval of a single feature.

  • F4: collective feature efficiency: proportion of samples that remain after the features have been used one after another to separate the classes.

Overlap, neighborhood based (they work with any number of classes; Ho & Basu, 2002; Leyva et al., 2015):

  • N1: proportion of samples that are connected to a sample of another class in the minimum spanning tree.

  • N2: ratio of the intra-class to the inter-class nearest neighbor distances, \(r / (1 + r)\).

  • N3: error rate of the leave-one-out 1-nearest neighbor classifier. N3_bal: the mean of its class-wise error rates (a class-balanced variant, not in Ho & Basu).

  • N4: error rate of the 1-nearest neighbor classifier on randomly interpolated samples (of the same class) (needs a random number stream, see seed).

  • LSC: local set cardinality, \(1 - \sum |LS| / n^2\).

Overlap and imbalance together:

  • R: R-value (Oh, 2011), the proportion of samples in the overlapping region (\(> theta\) of the k nearest neighbors from another class). For two classes it is \((IR \cdot R_{maj} + R_{min}) / (IR + 1)\), so it is dominated by the majority class.

  • R_aug: augmented R-value (Borsos et al., 2018), \((R_{maj} + IR \cdot R_{min}) / (IR + 1)\): the weights are swapped so that the minority class, which is more affected by overlap, is dominant. For more than two classes the class weights are \(n_{max} / n_k\) (normalized); this generalization is ours.

Noise, types of minority examples (Napierala & Stefanowski, 2016). The minority samples (all classes except the largest one) are labelled by the proportion \(s\) of their k nearest neighbors from their own class: safe (\(s \ge 0.8\)), borderline (\(0.4 \le s < 0.8\)), rare (\(0 < s < 0.4\)) and outlier (\(s = 0\)). With k = 5 these are 4-5, 2-3, 1 and 0 neighbors. The measures SAFE, BORDERLINE, RARE and OUTLIER are the proportions of minority samples of each type. Larger RARE and OUTLIER mean a noisier minority class.

References

Borsos, Z., Lemnaru, C., & Potolea, R. (2018). Dealing with overlap and imbalance: a new metric and approach. Pattern Analysis and Applications, 21(2), 381-395.

Ho, T. K., & Basu, M. (2002). Complexity measures of supervised classification problems. IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, 24(3), 289-300.

Leyva, E., Gonzalez, A., & Perez, R. (2015). A set of complexity measures designed for applying meta-learning to instance selection. IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering, 27(2), 354-367.

Lorena, A. C., Garcia, L. P., Lehmann, J., Souto, M. C., & Ho, T. K. (2019). How complex is your classification problem? A survey on measuring classification complexity. ACM Computing Surveys, 52(5), 1-34.

Napierala, K., & Stefanowski, J. (2016). Types of minority class examples and their influence on learning classifiers in imbalanced domains. Journal of Intelligent Information Systems, 46(3), 563-597.

Oh, S. (2011). A new dataset evaluation method based on category overlap. Computers in Biology and Medicine, 41(2), 115-122.

Orriols-Puig, A., Macia, N., & Ho, T. K. (2010). Documentation for the data complexity library in C++. Technical report, La Salle, Universitat Ramon Llull.

Ortigosa-Hernandez, J., Inza, I., & Lozano, J. A. (2017). Measuring the class-imbalance extent of multi-class problems. Pattern Recognition Letters, 98, 32-38.

Examples

set.seed(1)
x <- rbind(matrix(rnorm(400, 3, 1), ncol = 2), matrix(rnorm(40, 4, 1), ncol = 2))
y <- factor(rep(c("negative", "positive"), c(200, 20)))

complexity_IR(y = y)
#> [1] 10
complexity_R_aug(x, y)
#> [1] 0.9090909
complexity_N3(x, y)
#> [1] 0.1181818
